agent_scope: standalone technology nodes (api/lib/plugin/sdk) that do not inherit evidence from the method/tool/engine catalogs; all URLs HTTP-verified before inclusion

sources.title: DirectX 12 programming guide (Windows Win32)
sources.locator: Landing page of the Win32 Direct3D 12 programming guide section
sources.applicability_note: Authoritative vendor reference for the D3D12 programming model: command queues/lists, bundles, resource binding, fences and synchronization. normative for Windows PC targets.

sources.title: Command queues and command lists (Direct3D 12)
sources.locator: Section overview describing ID3D12CommandQueue / ID3D12CommandList and the ExecuteCommandLists submission model
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the claim that D3D12 submission is explicit and app-driven rather than driver-implicit.

sources.title: Direct3D 11 graphics (table of contents)
sources.locator: Table of contents of the Direct3D 11 graphics documentation set
sources.applicability_note: Defines the scope of the D3D11 API surface (devices, contexts, resources, shaders). Used as the normative reference for what D3D11 offers compared with D3D12.

sources.title: Direct3D 11 programming reference (Win32 API index)
sources.locator: API index page for the ID3D11Device / ID3D11DeviceContext interface family
sources.applicability_note: Interface-level reference. Confirms the immediate/deferred context object model that distinguishes D3D11 from the D3D12 command-list model.

sources.title: Vulkan Specification (latest, HTML)
sources.locator: Full normative specification document (vkspec.html)
sources.applicability_note: The normative, versioned specification. Highest available authority for Vulkan semantics; because 'latest' is rolling, version-specific claims must quote the target minor version.

sources.title: Vulkan-Docs (Khronos Group repository)
sources.locator: Repository root README describing the spec/refpages/XML sources
sources.applicability_note: Source-of-truth repository behind the published spec; useful for tracing a statement to a specific tagged release.

sources.title: DirectX Raytracing (DXR) functional specification overview
sources.locator: Overview section introducing raytracing pipelines, acceleration structures and shader stages
sources.applicability_note: Primary vendor reference for DXR concepts: bottom-level/top-level acceleration structures, ray generation / closest-hit / any-hit / miss shaders, shader tables.

sources.title: HLSL reference for DirectX Raytracing
sources.locator: Reference listing of raytracing-specific HLSL intrinsics and system-value semantics
sources.applicability_note: Interface-level proof that DXR is expressed through HLSL intrinsics (TraceRay, payload/attribute structures) rather than a separate language.

sources.title: acl - Animation Compression Library
sources.locator: Repository README: purpose, feature list and design goals
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for what ACL is and what it targets (animation clip compression and fast sampling). Any performance/ratio figure must be quoted from this README or the docs, not assumed.

sources.title: Animation Compression Library in Unreal Engine
sources.locator: Engine documentation page for the ACL plugin and its compression settings assets
sources.applicability_note: Confirms ACL is not merely a community library but is shipped with the engine; this is the strongest available adoption evidence for ACL.

sources.title: meshoptimizer - mesh optimization library
sources.locator: Repository root: algorithm list (index/vertex-cache/overdraw/fetch optimization, simplification, encoders)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the library's scope. Note it is a build-time/offline and load-time geometry processing library, not a runtime renderer component.

sources.title: meshoptimizer README
sources.locator: README body describing each algorithm, its purpose and its expected effect
sources.applicability_note: Detailed per-algorithm reference used to ground mechanism claims without quoting numbers that depend on the input mesh.

sources.title: RVO2 Library: documentation (2.0)
sources.author_or_publisher: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Gamma Lab
sources.locator: Documentation index and API reference for RVO2 2.0 (Agent, Simulator, KdTree)
sources.applicability_note: Primary reference implementation of the Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance (ORCA) algorithm for real-time multi-agent simulation. Academic, not a commercial middleware.

sources.title: RVO2 Library - project page
sources.locator: Project landing page with the abstract of the underlying ORCA paper
sources.applicability_note: States the research origin and licensing of the library; useful to distinguish the reference implementation from engine-vendor crowd products.

sources.title: Tracy Profiler
sources.platform: Windows / Linux / macOS, C++ (also C, Rust, Lua bindings)
sources.locator: Repository root describing the hybrid instrumentation + sampling profiler
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for Tracy's scope: frame profiler with manual zones, sampling, locks, GPU and memory profiling. A development tool, not a shipped runtime component.

sources.title: Tracy Profiler README
sources.locator: README describing features, supported GPU APIs and integration model
sources.applicability_note: Grounds claims about which graphics APIs Tracy can correlate (D3D11/12, OpenGL, Vulkan) and about its client/server architecture.

sources.title: Opus Codec - official site
sources.locator: Landing page stating the intended application range (VoIP, videoconferencing, in-game chat, live music)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source, and it explicitly names 'in-game chat' as a target application - which is what makes Opus a defensible default for in-game voice.

sources.title: RFC 6716 - Definition of the Opus Audio Codec
sources.locator: Normative RFC defining the codec, its modes (SILK/CELT hybrid) and algorithmic latency classes
sources.applicability_note: The normative specification: guarantees interoperability and pins down latency/quality properties that marketing pages do not.

sources.title: PhysX (NVIDIA-Omniverse) repository
sources.locator: Repository root: SDK scope, build instructions, feature summary
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the current open-source PhysX 5 SDK: rigid bodies, articulations, character controller, cooking, GPU acceleration.

sources.title: NVIDIA PhysX SDK developer page
sources.locator: Product page describing the SDK and its platform/feature coverage
sources.applicability_note: Vendor positioning page. Useful for supported-platform claims; less precise than the repository for behavioural detail.

sources.title: Unity DOTS product page
sources.locator: Product page defining DOTS as the combination of Entities, Burst, Jobs and the C# Job System
sources.applicability_note: Establishes that Entities/Burst/Jobs are one product family, so their version compatibility must be treated as coupled rather than independent.

sources.title: Unity Entities package manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page (ECS concepts, worlds, systems, baking)
sources.applicability_note: Normative reference for the ECS data model and the authoring/baking workflow.

sources.title: Unity Netcode for Entities manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page (client/server prediction, ghost replication)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the netcode feature set and its dependency on Entities and Transport.

sources.title: Unity Transport package manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page (connections, pipelines, drivers)
sources.applicability_note: Lower-level networking layer beneath Netcode; grounds claims about reliability/ordering pipelines.

sources.title: Unity Addressables package manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page (groups, labels, build and load by address)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the address-based asset loading model and remote-content workflow.

sources.title: Unity Burst compiler package manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page (LLVM backend, [BurstCompile], restrictions on managed code)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for what Burst can and cannot compile - the constraint that drives most DOTS adoption risk.

sources.title: Universal Render Pipeline package manual
sources.locator: Package documentation landing page for the Scriptable Render Pipeline implementation
sources.applicability_note: Grounds SRP claims on the concrete URP package rather than on the abstract SRP concept.

sources.title: World Partition in Unreal Engine
sources.locator: Documentation page describing the grid-based partitioning, streaming cells and One File Per Actor
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the World Partition streaming model and its OFPA collaboration requirement.

sources.title: Replication Graph in Unreal Engine
sources.locator: Documentation page describing the replication graph node classes and the motivation (large player counts)
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the claim that the default single-list replication does not scale and that the graph exists to make relevancy/dormancy explicit.

sources.title: Steamworks SDK documentation
sources.locator: SDK landing page listing the API surface and integration requirements
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for what the SDK provides (auth, matchmaking, stats, UGC, ICloud, inventory) and for the fact that integration is API-level rather than optional.

sources.title: Steamworks Features overview
sources.locator: Feature index page enumerating Steamworks subsystems
sources.applicability_note: Used to ground the breadth claim: Steamworks is a bundle of many independent subsystems, so 'doing Steamworks' is scoped per-subsystem, not all-or-nothing.

sources.title: Microsoft DirectStorage repository
sources.locator: Repository root: runtime + tools, GDeflate codec, staging buffer model
sources.applicability_note: Primary source for the API shape: queued bulk reads, decompression on GPU, explicit staging.

sources.title: DirectStorage README
sources.locator: README describing requirements, supported decompression codecs and the sample
sources.applicability_note: Grounds the hardware prerequisite claim (NVMe SSD class) and the GPU-decompression claim.

sources.title: Ashes of the Singularity (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article: release, developer, and engine/API notes
sources.applicability_note: Secondary encyclopedic source. Used only to establish that the title shipped and supported a DirectX 12 path; not used for any performance figure.

sources.title: Civilization VI (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article: release, developer, platforms
sources.applicability_note: Secondary encyclopedic source; establishes a second, independently-developed shipped title with a DirectX 12 render path.

sources.locator: Game article: release, developer, engine and platform notes

sources.title: Grand Theft Auto V (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article: PC release and engine notes
sources.applicability_note: Second, independently-developed shipped DirectX 11 title, from a different studio and genre than The Witcher 3.

sources.locator: Game article including the ray tracing / DXR section

sources.locator: Game article including the ray tracing technology section

sources.title: Batman: Arkham Asylum (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including the PhysX technology notes
sources.applicability_note: Documents a shipped title whose PC version used NVIDIA PhysX for GPU-accelerated effects.

sources.title: Mafia II (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including the PhysX technology notes
sources.applicability_note: Second, independently-developed shipped title with prominent PhysX integration; different studio and genre from Batman: Arkham Asylum.

sources.title: Team Fortress 2 (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including engine (Source) and platform notes
sources.applicability_note: Used to establish a long-lived shipped Source-engine multiplayer title whose voice chat is part of the shipped feature set; combined with the Opus codec claim about Source voice.

sources.title: Counter-Strike 2 (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including engine (Source 2) and release/platform notes
sources.applicability_note: Second, distinct Valve multiplayer title on Source 2; used for voice-codec and Steamworks runtime-integration evidence.

sources.title: Fortnite (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including engine (Unreal Engine) and mode (Battle Royale) notes
sources.applicability_note: Establishes the shipped title that motivated Unreal's large-player-count networking work; also a shipped Unreal Engine 5 title.

sources.title: V Rising (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article: developer (Stunlock Studios), engine (Unity), release
sources.applicability_note: A shipped Unity title from a studio that publicly used the DOTS/ECS stack; used as the concrete shipped example for the Unity DOTS packages.

sources.title: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including the PC port technology notes
sources.applicability_note: Documents a shipped Windows port whose loading path was built on high-speed SSD streaming; used only as a streaming-IO example, not as a DirectStorage API proof.

sources.title: Forspoken (Wikipedia)
sources.locator: Game article including the PC technology/streaming notes
sources.applicability_note: Documents an early shipped Windows title that shipped with DirectStorage-based IO.

claims.statement: Direct3D 12 moves work submission under explicit application control: the application creates command queues, records command lists and submits them via ExecuteCommandLists, instead of the driver translating immediate-mode calls at draw time.
claims.locator: Programming guide, command submission section (ID3D12CommandQueue / ID3D12CommandList / ExecuteCommandLists)
claims.context: This is the architectural difference that determines how much CPU-side driver cost a project can remove, and how much synchronization work it inherits.

claims.statement: Command lists are allocated from command allocators and can be recorded on multiple threads and submitted to a single queue, so parallel command recording is an explicit, application-owned responsibility rather than a driver behaviour.
claims.locator: Section 'Command queues and command lists': multi-engine / parallel recording and submission model
claims.context: Directly relevant to the multithreaded-render-queue method; also the source of the main correctness risk (allocators must not be reset while in flight).

claims.statement: Because state validation is performed when a Pipeline State Object is created rather than at every draw, D3D12 reduces per-draw driver overhead but requires PSOs to be created (and ideally pre-cached) before they are needed.
claims.locator: Programming guide, pipeline state section
claims.context: This is the mechanism behind pipeline-state-object pre-caching as a separate work item: the API trades per-draw cost for up-front creation cost.

claims.statement: Resource state transitions and lifetime/ hazard tracking become the application's responsibility; every transition must be expressed as a resource barrier, and incorrect barriers produce silent corruption or GPU hangs rather than a driver-managed safe state.
claims.locator: Programming guide, resource barriers / synchronization section
claims.context: The dominant engineering cost of adopting D3D12. It is a correctness burden, not a performance feature.

game_examples.fact: Shipped as one of the first commercial PC titles with a DirectX 12 render path, and was widely used as an early D3D12 API showcase; the game's strategy scale (very large unit counts) is the workload the explicit-submission model targets.
game_examples.locator: Game article: development/technology and release sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates that a small studio shipped a D3D12 path early and that the payoff was concentrated in CPU-bound, high-object-count scenes.
game_examples.non_transferable: Oxide wrote its own engine and controlled the renderer completely; a licensed-engine project cannot assume the same access to the submission layer, and Nitrous' results do not transfer to a different scene composition.

game_examples.fact: Shipped with a DirectX 12 render path selectable on Windows, from a different studio and a turn-based (not real-time-strategy) workload, showing D3D12 adoption was not limited to one engine house.
game_examples.locator: Game article: release and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: A second independent shipped data point: D3D12 was adopted in a mainstream, non-shooter, non-graphically-aggressive title as well.
game_examples.non_transferable: Civ VI's render path choice does not show how much CPU headroom D3D12 bought; no measured comparison is available from this source, so it cannot be used as evidence of a speedup.

claims.statement: Direct3D 11 is built around a device plus immediate and deferred contexts: rendering calls are issued through ID3D11DeviceContext and the runtime/driver performs state tracking and resource hazard management on the application's behalf.
claims.locator: API index: ID3D11Device and ID3D11DeviceContext interface family
claims.context: This implicit management is the reason D3D11 has lower CPU-scaling ceiling but far lower implementation risk than D3D12.

claims.statement: Direct3D 11 remains available on Windows 7 SP1 and later, so it is the retained fallback path for a project that must still support older Windows installations.
claims.locator: Direct3D 11 graphics documentation set, platform requirements
claims.context: Relevant to the target-platform decision: choosing D3D12-only removes Windows 7 from the addressable install base.

claims.statement: Because the driver performs validation and hazard tracking at call time, D3D11 draw-call submission carries higher per-call CPU overhead, which is why D3D11 titles are typically limited by CPU submission before they are limited by GPU throughput in high-object-count scenes.
claims.locator: API index: immediate context submission model
claims.context: Qualitative mechanism statement. No per-call microsecond figure is claimed because the cited reference does not publish one.

game_examples.fact: A shipped open-world PC title whose Windows version targeted DirectX 11, demonstrating that large-scale streaming open worlds were delivered on the implicit-context model.
game_examples.locator: Game article: technology and release sections
game_examples.relevance: Shows D3D11 is sufficient for a large open world at high visual quality - it is not only a low-end or legacy option.
game_examples.non_transferable: REDengine 3 is a bespoke engine with heavy engine-level investment; the result does not transfer to a project that cannot afford equivalent renderer engineering.

game_examples.fact: The Windows release shipped on DirectX 11 from a different studio and genre, giving a second independent shipped example of a AAA PC title on the D3D11 path.
game_examples.locator: Game article: PC release and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Confirms D3D11 as the mainstream shipping path for AAA PC titles at the time.
game_examples.non_transferable: RAGE's own deferred pipeline and streaming design do the heavy lifting; the API choice alone does not explain the result.

claims.statement: Vulkan is an explicit, cross-platform graphics and compute API: the application is responsible for synchronization, memory allocation and resource state management, and shaders are consumed in the SPIR-V intermediate representation.
claims.locator: Vulkan specification, fundamentals and synchronization/memory allocation chapters
claims.context: Same explicit-control trade-off as D3D12, but with a portable API surface across Windows, Linux and Android.

claims.statement: Because the specification is versioned and the published 'latest' document is a rolling target, a project must pin the Vulkan minor version it targets rather than coding against 'latest'.
claims.locator: vkspec.html header / version banner
claims.context: A real project risk: claims valid for one Vulkan minor version are not automatically valid for another.

claims.statement: The normative sources of the specification are published as a versioned repository, so a statement can be traced to a specific tagged release rather than to a mutable web page.
claims.locator: Vulkan-Docs repository root and tag list
claims.context: Useful for the evidence discipline of this study: it lets a Vulkan claim be pinned to a tag instead of a moving document.

claims.statement: Vulkan's explicit memory and descriptor management shifts allocation strategy onto the application, which is why engine-side sub-allocators and descriptor pooling are usually prerequisite work rather than optional optimisation.
claims.locator: Vulkan specification, resource creation and descriptor set chapters
claims.context: Directly affects the work-package estimate: adopting Vulkan adds allocator and descriptor-pool engineering before any rendering benefit appears.

game_examples.fact: Shipped with a Vulkan render path alongside OpenGL and was one of the first major commercial PC titles to do so, from a studio with direct control of its renderer.
game_examples.locator: Game article: development and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Establishes Vulkan as a shipped, not experimental, PC API for a AAA title.
game_examples.non_transferable: id Software owns its renderer end to end and had a history of low-level API work; the effort required is not representative for a team adopting Vulkan into an existing engine.

game_examples.fact: A later shipped id Software title whose PC renderer is Vulkan-based, providing a second data point from the same series but a different engine generation.
game_examples.locator: Game article: technology section
game_examples.relevance: Shows Vulkan persisted as the chosen PC path across an engine generation, not a one-off experiment.
game_examples.non_transferable: Both examples come from the same studio, so they share methodology and staffing; they do not independently validate Vulkan adoption cost for a different organisation.

claims.statement: DirectX Raytracing extends Direct3D 12 with a raytracing pipeline whose stages are ray generation, closest-hit, any-hit, intersection and miss shaders, and with explicit bottom-level and top-level acceleration structures describing scene geometry.
claims.locator: DXR overview: raytracing pipeline and acceleration structure sections
claims.context: This is why ray tracing costs are dominated by acceleration-structure build and update time, not only by shading.

claims.statement: DXR requires GPU hardware with the corresponding raytracing tier; it is not available on all Direct3D 12 devices, so a DXR feature must be gated behind a capability query and need a non-DXR fallback path.
claims.locator: DXR overview: hardware/feature tier requirements
claims.context: Directly relevant to the target-platform decision: a DXR-dependent look cannot be the only path for a game that must run on older GPUs.

claims.statement: Ray traversal is expressed through HLSL intrinsics and payload/attribute structures inside the existing HLSL/D3D12 toolchain, rather than through a separate shading language.
claims.locator: HLSL raytracing reference: TraceRay-related intrinsics and system-value semantics
claims.context: Lowers the integration barrier at the language level, but does not lower the cost of building and maintaining acceleration structures.

claims.statement: Ray-traced effects are normally applied selectively (reflections, shadows, ambient occlusion, or GI at reduced resolution) rather than replacing rasterisation wholesale, because traversal cost scales with rays and scene complexity.
claims.locator: DXR overview: usage guidance for selective ray-traced effects
claims.context: Supports the 'selective ray-traced effects' method in the catalog; no frame-cost figure is claimed.

game_examples.fact: Shipped with real-time ray traced reflections using DXR and was among the first retail titles to do so, with the effect scoped to reflections rather than to full GI.
game_examples.locator: Game article: ray tracing section
game_examples.relevance: Concrete shipped proof that a selective DXR effect (reflections only) was viable in a large-scale multiplayer title.
game_examples.non_transferable: DICE scoped DXR to reflections and offered quality tiers; the cost profile of that choice does not transfer to full-scene GI or to a different scene composition.

game_examples.fact: Shipped with DXR-based ray traced global illumination, a different and heavier use of the API than reflections only, from an independent studio.
game_examples.locator: Game article: ray tracing / technology section
game_examples.relevance: Second, distinct shipped DXR example showing a different effect class (GI) and a different engine.
game_examples.non_transferable: Metro Exodus' GI implementation assumes its own lighting model and level density; the result does not generalise to open-world scenes with different light counts.

claims.statement: ACL is an animation compression library whose stated purpose is to reduce the memory footprint of animation clips while keeping clip sampling fast, which are two competing objectives in animation systems.
claims.locator: Repository README: introduction and design goals
claims.context: Relevant to the animation-compression method: the trade-off is between memory and sampling cost, and the library is explicit about both.

claims.statement: ACL is shipped with Unreal Engine as an engine-provided plugin rather than only as a third-party download, which makes it available without an external integration step in UE.
claims.locator: Engine documentation page for the Animation Compression Library plugin
claims.context: This is the strongest adoption signal available for ACL and materially lowers the integration risk for a UE-based project.

claims.statement: In Unreal Engine the library is surfaced through compression settings assets that pre-configure bone and curve compression, so it is selected as a codec rather than called directly by game code.
claims.locator: Engine documentation: compression settings assets location and usage
claims.context: Practical consequence: switching to ACL in UE is a content-pipeline configuration change, plus re-compression of existing animation assets.

claims.statement: No primary source located in this study names a specific shipped commercial title that uses ACL; the located evidence establishes engine-level availability (Unreal Engine) and library purpose, but not per-title adoption.
claims.locator: Repository README - no shipped-title list published
claims.context: Declared honestly rather than inferred. Under the study's rules, absence of a source is not evidence of adoption.

claims.statement: meshoptimizer provides geometry optimisation algorithms - index/vertex-cache optimisation, overdraw optimisation, vertex-fetch optimisation, vertex quantisation, mesh simplification and index/vertex encoders - as a C/C++ library.
claims.locator: Repository root: algorithm/feature list
claims.context: This is a mesh-processing library; it changes the data fed to the GPU, not the rendering algorithm.

claims.statement: The library is primarily a build-time and load-time tool: its optimisations are applied to mesh data before or during loading, and the encoder/decoder pair is used to keep the data compressed in transit and at rest.
claims.locator: README: per-algorithm description and encoder/decoder usage
claims.context: Important for the load-profile model: it reduces GPU vertex-fetch cost and asset size, and it adds CPU time at build/load, not per-frame.

claims.statement: The benefit of each optimisation is input-dependent: vertex-cache and overdraw improvements depend on the mesh's index order and topology, so no single percentage gain applies across a project's asset set.
claims.locator: README: notes on expected results per algorithm
claims.context: Deliberately no numeric claim. Quoting a fixed percentage would exceed what the source supports.

claims.statement: No primary source located in this study names a specific shipped commercial title that ships meshoptimizer; because it is a build/load-time library it is typically invisible in a shipped build, which makes per-title evidence structurally hard to obtain.
claims.locator: Repository root - no shipped-title list published
claims.context: Declared gap. The absence is explained by the tool's build-time nature, but it is still an absence of proof.

claims.statement: RVO2 is the reference implementation of Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance (ORCA) for real-time multi-agent simulation: each agent selects a velocity inside a set of half-plane constraints derived from the other agents, producing local avoidance without central coordination.
claims.locator: RVO2 2.0 documentation: Simulator / Agent classes and the ORCA algorithm description
claims.context: Relevant to the rvo_local_avoidance method: it is a local, per-agent solution and does not by itself do global path planning.

claims.statement: RVO2 originates from academic work at UNC Chapel Hill's Gamma Lab and is published as a reference implementation with its documentation, rather than as a maintained commercial middleware product.
claims.locator: Project landing page: abstract and licensing
claims.context: A project risk: using a research reference implementation means owning maintenance, platform ports and debugging in-house.

claims.statement: The library is delivered as C++ with a C# binding and exposes a Simulator that owns agents and a spatial structure (KdTree) for neighbour queries, so neighbour-search cost grows with agent density and must be budgeted separately from the ORCA solve.
claims.locator: RVO2 2.0 documentation: Simulator and KdTree classes
claims.context: Directly supports the agent-update-budget method: the avoidance solve is not the only cost.

claims.statement: No primary source located in this study documents RVO2 specifically inside a named shipped commercial title; the library is widely used in prototypes and in engine integrations, but that usage is not the same as verified per-title proof.
claims.locator: Project page - no shipped-title list published
claims.context: Declared gap. Crowd avoidance behaviour observable in shipped games is not evidence that RVO2 in particular was used.

claims.statement: Tracy is a hybrid profiler: it combines manual instrumentation zones with statistical sampling and adds lock, GPU and memory profiling, so a single timeline can show CPU zones, GPU work and allocation activity together.
claims.locator: Repository root: feature description
claims.context: Relevant to the profiling/observability work packages: it replaces several separate tools with one correlated timeline.

claims.statement: Tracy is a client/server profiler: the game links a client that records zones and streams them to a separate viewer application, so instrumentation cost is paid in the build under test and the viewer cost is off-target.
claims.locator: README: client/server architecture and integration model
claims.context: Practical consequence: a profiled build is not the shipping build, so measured numbers are build-configuration dependent.

claims.statement: Tracy can correlate GPU timestamps for the major PC graphics APIs, which is what allows a CPU zone and the GPU work it submitted to be seen on one timeline.
claims.locator: README: supported graphics APIs / GPU profiling section
claims.context: This is the property that makes GPU-vs-CPU attribution claims possible at all; without it, frame-time attribution stays guesswork.

claims.statement: Tracy is a development-time tool and is not shipped inside retail builds, so a shipped-title example is not an applicable form of proof for this node. This is declared instead of being filled with a substitute example.
claims.locator: Repository root - tool classified as a development profiler
claims.context: Declared non-applicable. Forcing a game example here would be a category error, not evidence.

claims.statement: Opus is a lossy audio codec standardised as RFC 6716 that combines the SILK (speech) and CELT (general audio) coding layers in a hybrid mode, letting one codec cover both narrowband speech and fullband music.
claims.locator: RFC 6716: codec definition and SILK/CELT hybrid description
claims.context: This is why a single codec can serve both voice chat and in-game audio streams, avoiding two codec integrations.

claims.statement: The codec's official site explicitly names in-game chat among its target applications, alongside VoIP and videoconferencing.
claims.locator: opus-codec.org landing page: application list
claims.context: Direct applicability note, not an inference: voice chat is a stated target of the codec.

claims.statement: Opus supports algorithmic latency classes suited to interactive conversation, which is the property that makes it usable for real-time voice rather than only for stored audio.
claims.locator: RFC 6716: latency / frame-size configuration section
claims.context: No single latency figure is quoted, because the achievable latency depends on the configured frame size and application settings.

game_examples.fact: A long-lived shipped Source-engine multiplayer title whose in-game voice chat is part of the delivered feature set, giving a concrete context in which an interactive speech codec is required at scale.
game_examples.locator: Game article: features and multiplayer sections
game_examples.relevance: Establishes the gameplay context that creates the requirement (many concurrent speakers, low latency), which is what makes codec choice a decision at all.
game_examples.non_transferable: This example proves the requirement exists, not that Opus specifically was the codec used in this title at release.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Source 2 multiplayer title with in-game voice chat, providing a second shipped context for interactive speech coding in a competitive (latency-sensitive) setting.
game_examples.locator: Game article: features and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Second shipped data point in the genre where voice latency is most visible.
game_examples.non_transferable: Same limitation: the shipped game demonstrates the requirement, not the specific codec implementation.

claims.statement: PhysX is a physics SDK covering rigid bodies, articulations, a character controller and collision/cooking pipelines, published as an open-source SDK with GPU acceleration support.
claims.locator: Repository root: SDK scope and feature summary
claims.context: Relevant to the broadphase/multithreaded-physics methods: the SDK owns the broadphase and solver, so engine-side tuning is limited to its exposed parameters.

claims.statement: The SDK targets Windows, Linux and macOS as well as console platforms, so it is usable as a single physics backend across a multi-platform PC-first release.
claims.locator: Developer page: platform coverage
claims.context: Reduces the risk of needing a second physics backend per platform.

claims.statement: PhysX's solver behaviour is version-dependent and its GPU-accelerated paths are not a deterministic-lockstep substrate, so it cannot be assumed to satisfy a deterministic networking model without explicit verification on the target build.
claims.locator: Repository root: SDK build/feature description (no determinism guarantee stated)
claims.context: Stated as a risk arising from the absence of a determinism guarantee in the primary source, not as a measured result.

game_examples.fact: A shipped title whose PC version used NVIDIA PhysX for GPU-accelerated physics effects, showing the SDK integrated into a retail release as an effects-layer component.
game_examples.locator: Game article: technology / PhysX section
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates shipped, retail use of the middleware with visible gameplay effects.
game_examples.non_transferable: The integration was an effects layer on top of the game's own systems, not the core gameplay physics; results do not transfer to a fully PhysX-driven simulation.

game_examples.fact: A shipped title from a different studio and genre that also shipped prominent PhysX integration on PC, giving a second independent example.
game_examples.locator: Game article: technology / PhysX section
game_examples.relevance: Shows PhysX was adopted across multiple unrelated studios in the same period.
game_examples.non_transferable: Same scope limitation: effects-layer integration, not a full physics rewrite.

claims.statement: Unity Entities is the ECS package of the DOTS family: data is laid out in archetype-based chunks and iterated by systems, with an authoring-to-runtime baking step that converts authored scenes into entity data.
claims.locator: Package manual: ECS concepts, worlds, systems and baking
claims.context: Relevant to the ecs_data_oriented_crowd method: the performance story comes from memory layout and batch iteration, not from a faster language.

claims.statement: Entities is not standalone - it is one component of the DOTS product family alongside the C# Job System and the Burst compiler, so its version compatibility must be evaluated together with those packages rather than independently.
claims.locator: DOTS product page: family composition
claims.context: This coupling is the main source of version-conflict risk in a Unity DOTS stack and must appear as a coupled dependency in the graph.

claims.statement: Adopting Entities is an architecture-level decision: gameplay code must be written against the data model (components/systems) rather than against GameObjects, so existing GameObject-based code does not automatically benefit.
claims.locator: Package manual: authoring/baking workflow
claims.context: Directly affects the work-package estimate: migration, not adoption, dominates the cost.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity title from a studio that built its simulation on the DOTS/ECS stack, giving a concrete retail example of the Entities package in production.
game_examples.locator: Game article: developer, engine and release sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates the Entities package sustaining a commercial survival game with large numbers of simulated entities.
game_examples.non_transferable: The studio had prior DOTS experience and built for it from the start; a mid-project migration would carry a different cost profile that this example does not measure.

game_examples.fact: Not a Unity title, and therefore used as a contrast case: it shows that large-entity-count simulation at retail scale is also delivered with a different engine and data model, so Entities is a means rather than a prerequisite.
game_examples.locator: Game article: engine and scale sections
game_examples.relevance: Guards against over-attributing the outcome to the package: the same class of problem is solved outside Unity's DOTS.
game_examples.non_transferable: This is deliberately a contrast example, not a use of the package; it cannot be counted as adoption evidence for Entities.

claims.statement: Netcode for Entities is a client/server netcode package built on top of Entities: it replicates 'ghosts' (entity snapshots) and provides client prediction and server-authoritative rollback.
claims.locator: Package manual: ghost replication, prediction and rollback sections
claims.context: Relevant to the client_prediction_reconciliation method: prediction correctness depends on the simulation being re-runnable, which is the hard part.

claims.statement: The package depends on the Entities package and on the Unity Transport package, so its supported versions are constrained by both and cannot be upgraded in isolation.
claims.locator: Package manual: package dependencies
claims.context: A concrete version-coupling that belongs in the dependency-conflict matrix.

claims.statement: Prediction and rollback require the simulated code to be deterministic enough to re-run; this constrains gameplay code much more than the transport layer does.
claims.locator: Package manual: prediction section and its requirements
claims.context: The dominant adoption risk. It is a constraint on game code, not a configuration option.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity multiplayer title built on the DOTS stack, providing a retail example where the Entities-side networking approach carries real player counts and world state.
game_examples.locator: Game article: multiplayer and release sections
game_examples.relevance: Shows the DOTS networking stack sustaining a commercial multiplayer release.
game_examples.non_transferable: The studio's prior DOTS investment and its specific simulation determinism do not transfer to a different team's codebase.

game_examples.fact: Used as a contrast case: a competitive multiplayer title that delivers sub-tick input responsiveness with rollback/netcode techniques on an entirely different engine, showing that the technique class is general while the Unity package is one implementation of it.
game_examples.locator: Game article: networking / subtick technology section
game_examples.relevance: Separates the method (prediction/rollback) from the specific package implementation.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; it is not evidence of the Unity package being used.

claims.statement: Unity Transport is the lower-level networking layer beneath Netcode: it provides connections, drivers and a configurable pipeline of stages for reliability, ordering and fragmentation.
claims.locator: Package manual: connections, drivers and pipelines
claims.context: Relevant because it lets a project choose per-channel guarantees instead of accepting one global transport behaviour.

claims.statement: Because reliability and sequencing are expressed as pipeline stages, the bandwidth and latency trade-off is a configuration decision per channel rather than a fixed engine property.
claims.locator: Package manual: pipeline stages
claims.context: Directly supports the network-relevancy and delta-compression methods: the transport can be tuned, but tuning it correctly requires measurement.

claims.statement: Transport is a dependency of Netcode for Entities, so its version is constrained by the netcode package's supported range even though it can also be used standalone.
claims.locator: Package manual: package dependencies
claims.context: Concrete coupling for the dependency graph.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity multiplayer title whose networking runs on the DOTS/Transport layer, giving a retail example of this transport carrying a commercial game.
game_examples.locator: Game article: multiplayer and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates the transport layer in a shipped, persistent-world multiplayer game.
game_examples.non_transferable: The game's specific channel configuration and tick rates are not published here, so the example does not validate a particular pipeline setup.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a competitive multiplayer title that solves the same latency/ordering problem with its own networking stack, showing the transport is a means to per-channel guarantees rather than the only way to get them.
game_examples.locator: Game article: networking technology section
game_examples.relevance: Prevents over-attributing a networking outcome to this specific package.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of Unity Transport being used in this title.

claims.statement: Addressables replaces direct scene/asset references with address-based loading: assets are organised into groups and bundles and are requested by address or label at runtime.
claims.locator: Package manual: groups, labels and address-based loading
claims.context: This is the mechanism that decouples content layout from load order, which is what makes remote/patched content possible.

claims.statement: Because assets are loaded asynchronously by address and referenced through handles, the caller must manage lifetimes explicitly; failing to release a handle keeps the bundle resident.
claims.locator: Package manual: loading and releasing assets
claims.context: A concrete operational risk: addressables shifts memory management from the scene graph to explicit handle discipline.

claims.statement: Content is built into bundles by group, so build time, patch granularity and download size are outcomes of how groups are configured rather than of the package alone.
claims.locator: Package manual: build and remote content sections
claims.context: Relevant to differential patching and build-size budgets: the grouping strategy is the decision, not the package.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity title whose content pipeline is organised for a persistent world with streamed content, giving a retail context for address-based asset loading.
game_examples.locator: Game article: engine, content and release sections
game_examples.relevance: Shows the address-based model sustaining a commercial Unity release with ongoing content updates.
game_examples.non_transferable: The example does not disclose the project's grouping strategy, so it cannot validate a specific bundle layout.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a shipped title with a heavily chunked, remotely patched content model on a different engine, demonstrating that address-based packaging is a general pattern rather than a Unity-specific capability.
game_examples.locator: Game article: content/update model sections
game_examples.relevance: Separates the pattern from the package implementation.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of Unity Addressables being used.

claims.statement: Burst is a compiler that translates a restricted subset of C# (applied via [BurstCompile]) to native code through an LLVM backend, so job code can run without the managed runtime overhead of the C# interpreter/JIT path.
claims.locator: Package manual: [BurstCompile] and LLVM backend
claims.context: Relevant to the GC/alloc budget methods: the win comes from native compilation of job code, not from C# becoming generally faster.

claims.statement: Burst cannot compile arbitrary C#: managed objects, most of the standard library and exception-heavy code are excluded, so code must be written against the supported subset to be compiled.
claims.locator: Package manual: supported language features and restrictions
claims.context: The dominant constraint: it forces a data-oriented coding style on the hot path and is a training cost for the team.

claims.statement: Burst is part of the DOTS family and is used by Entities to compile its job code, so its version is coupled to the Entities package in practice.
claims.locator: DOTS product page: family composition
claims.context: Concrete coupling for the dependency graph.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity title built on DOTS, where the hot-path simulation code is compiled with Burst, giving a retail example of the compiler in a commercial build.
game_examples.locator: Game article: engine and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates Burst sustaining a shipped simulation-heavy title.
game_examples.non_transferable: No per-system speedup is published here, so the example does not quantify the benefit.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a shipped title achieving large-scale simulation performance with native C++ on another engine, showing native compilation is the general technique and Burst is Unity's route to it inside C#.
game_examples.locator: Game article: engine and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Separates the technique from the package.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of Burst being used.

claims.statement: The Scriptable Render Pipeline is the Unity architecture that lets the render loop be defined in C# and scheduled by the engine; URP is the shipped, supported SRP implementation targeting scalable performance across platforms.
claims.locator: URP package manual: pipeline overview
claims.context: Relevant to the deferred/forward-plus decision: the pipeline determines what passes exist and therefore which lighting methods are available.

claims.statement: Because the render loop is scriptable, a project can customise passes - but every customisation is code that must be maintained against engine upgrades, rather than a supported configuration.
claims.locator: URP package manual: custom passes / extensibility
claims.context: The trade-off behind SRP: flexibility is bought with long-term maintenance ownership.

claims.statement: Render pipeline choice is effectively irreversible mid-project because materials, shaders and post-processing stacks are pipeline-specific, so it is an early architectural decision rather than a tunable one.
claims.locator: URP package manual: pipeline asset and shader compatibility
claims.context: This is why SRP selection belongs on the critical path for a Unity project.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unity title using a scriptable render pipeline, giving a retail example of a customised pipeline sustaining a commercial release.
game_examples.locator: Game article: engine and visual technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Shows an SRP-based Unity title shipping at commercial scale.
game_examples.non_transferable: The specific pipeline configuration is not published here, so it does not validate a particular pas structure.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a shipped title with a fully bespoke render pipeline on its own engine, showing that pipeline control - not the Unity package - is the underlying requirement for a distinctive look at high performance.
game_examples.locator: Game article: technology section
game_examples.relevance: Separates the architectural principle from the Unity implementation.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of Unity SRP being used.

claims.statement: World Partition replaces manual level streaming with an automatic grid-based system: the world is divided into cells that are streamed in and out based on streaming sources, so streaming is derived from world layout rather than authored per-level.
claims.locator: Documentation page: grid partitioning and streaming cells
claims.context: Relevant to the world_partition_streaming method: it changes where the streaming work happens - from level design to runtime cell management.

claims.statement: World Partition is paired with One File Per Actor, which stores each actor in its own file so multiple developers can edit the same world region without conflicting on a single map file.
claims.locator: Documentation page: One File Per Actor section
claims.context: A team-scaling property, not a rendering property: it removes a version-control bottleneck for large teams.

claims.statement: Streaming behaviour becomes a function of cell size, streaming-source configuration and data layers, so tuning is a configuration and budgeting exercise rather than a one-time setup.
claims.locator: Documentation page: streaming sources and data layers
claims.context: Directly feeds the load-profile and streaming-budget work packages.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unreal Engine title with a large, continuously updated world, giving a retail example of the partitioning/streaming approach at very large scale.
game_examples.locator: Game article: world, updates and engine sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates the streaming model sustaining a large, frequently updated live world.
game_examples.non_transferable: Epic develops the system alongside the game and has engine-level support; a licensee's tuning effort is not represented by this example.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a large streaming open world delivered on a different engine with a hand-authored streaming scheme, showing that the underlying requirement - distance-based world streaming - predates and is independent of World Partition.
game_examples.locator: Game article: world design and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Separates the requirement from the Unreal implementation.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of World Partition being used.

claims.statement: The Replication Graph replaces the engine's default 'check every actor against every connection' relevancy test with an explicit graph of node classes, so relevancy, prioritisation and dormancy are expressed as graph structure instead of per-actor checks.
claims.locator: Documentation page: motivation and node-class overview
claims.context: The algorithmic claim is a change of complexity class in the relevancy test: from connection-times-actor work to graph traversal.

claims.statement: The documentation motivates the graph by large player/actor counts, so it is a scaling feature for many-connection or many-actor games rather than a benefit for small scenes.
claims.locator: Documentation page: motivation section
claims.context: Important scoping: adopting it for a small co-op game would add complexity without the matching payoff.

claims.statement: The graph must be configured and maintained per game: node layout encodes the game's own notion of relevancy, so it is ongoing engineering tied to gameplay rather than a one-off setup.
claims.locator: Documentation page: node classes and configuration
claims.context: This is why the graph appears as a risk item: it is bespoke per project and must evolve with the game.

game_examples.fact: A shipped Unreal Engine battle-royale title with large simultaneous player counts and a large replicated actor set - the workload class the Replication Graph was created for.
game_examples.locator: Game article: battle royale mode and engine sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates the relevancy-scaling problem being solved at retail in the genre that motivated the feature.
game_examples.non_transferable: Epic co-developed the feature with this title and has engine-source access; a licensee's integration cost is not represented.

game_examples.fact: Contrast case: a competitive multiplayer title solving the same relevancy/actor-count problem on a different engine, confirming that per-connection relevancy filtering is a general requirement rather than a Unreal-specific one.
game_examples.locator: Game article: networking technology section
game_examples.relevance: Separates the requirement from the Unreal implementation.
game_examples.non_transferable: Contrast example only; not evidence of the Replication Graph being used.

claims.statement: Steamworks is an SDK integrated at API level into the shipping build, providing authentication, matchmaking, stats/achievements, user-generated content, cloud storage and inventory services.
claims.locator: SDK documentation landing page: API surface and integration
claims.context: Relevant because it makes several otherwise custom back-end systems available as a single integration, which is a large scope reduction for a small team.

claims.statement: Steamworks is a bundle of largely independent subsystems rather than one monolithic feature, so a project can adopt individual subsystems (for example auth and achievements) without adopting all of them.
claims.locator: Features overview: enumerated subsystems
claims.context: This is why 'integrate Steamworks' is not one work package: each subsystem has its own effort and risk profile.

claims.statement: Because the SDK is linked into the shipping build and calls into the Steam client at runtime, it couples the game's launch path to the Steam client, which is a platform dependency rather than an optional convenience.
claims.locator: SDK documentation: integration requirements
claims.context: A portability risk: removing or replacing it later is a non-trivial change to the build and launch path.

game_examples.fact: A shipped multiplayer title distributed through Steam with Steam-level identity, matchmaking and inventory, demonstrating the SDK's subsystems in a live commercial title.
game_examples.locator: Game article: distribution, monetisation and technology sections
game_examples.relevance: Shows the deepest end of Steamworks integration (inventory/economy) working at scale.
game_examples.non_transferable: Valve owns both the game and the platform, so a third party's integration effort and constraints differ.

game_examples.fact: A second, long-lived shipped multiplayer title using Steamworks subsystems including the item economy and cloud-backed features, showing the integration persists across a very long operational lifetime.
game_examples.locator: Game article: distribution and economy sections
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates long-term maintainability of a Steamworks integration.
game_examples.non_transferable: Same first-party limitation as above; both examples are Valve titles.

claims.statement: DirectStorage provides a queued, bulk-read IO API for games: requests are submitted to a queue and completed asynchronously in bulk, replacing many small synchronous reads with batched ones.
claims.locator: Repository root: API shape, staging buffer and queue model
claims.context: Relevant to the load-profile model: the benefit is fewer, larger IO submissions and less CPU spent per byte, not a faster disk.

claims.statement: The SDK targets high-speed NVMe-class storage; it is not a general improvement for mechanical or SATA-bound IO paths, so its benefit is conditional on the user's storage device.
claims.locator: README: system requirements
claims.context: Critical for the hardware basket decision: a DirectStorage path must have a fallback for users below the requirement.

claims.statement: Compressed assets can be decompressed by the GPU rather than by the CPU, which moves decompression off the main IO/CPU path and changes where the cost of asset loading appears.
claims.locator: README: decompression / GDeflate support
claims.context: This is why GPU decompression interacts with the GPU budget: it trades CPU time for GPU time.

game_examples.fact: An early shipped Windows title that used DirectStorage for its asset loading path, giving a retail example of the SDK in a shipped build.
game_examples.locator: Game article: PC technology / streaming section
game_examples.relevance: Demonstrates the SDK reached shipping builds rather than remaining a sample-only API.
game_examples.non_transferable: No measured load-time improvement is available from this source, so the example does not quantify the benefit.

game_examples.fact: The Windows port of a title designed around instant world transitions, shipped with a high-speed-SSD streaming path, giving a second example of the loading pattern DirectStorage targets.
game_examples.locator: Game article: PC port technology section
game_examples.relevance: Shows the design pattern (SSD-dependent instant transitions) validated on PC hardware.
game_examples.non_transferable: The PC port's specific IO implementation is not fully documented here; this is evidence of the pattern, not proof of the API being used.
